title: Choose fabric for a useful pouch
outcome: TEXTILES: choose fabric and technique for a purpose.
goal: I can choose fabric and a joining method for a pouch and explain how they suit its job.
success: I can link a fabric property to the pouch purpose.
I can compare joining methods and choose one.
I can record my own choice and a reason for next week.
purpose: Design a small reusable pouch for three paper prompt cards. Each card is 60 mm wide and 80 mm high. Hold the cards upright. Join the sides and bottom; leave the top open. The pouch should be comfortable to handle, with no loose sharp parts.
dimensions: Default plan: two fabric rectangles, each 100 mm wide and 120 mm high. This is 10 cm by 12 cm. Plan a seam line 10 mm inside the left, right and bottom edges. Leave the top open. These are written measurements, not a printed cutting template.
model_choice: Adult model: non-fraying felt with hand running stitch. Its firm shape could help hold the cards. Stitch joins the sides and bottom without an adhesive cure wait. Check the actual felt and tools before making. Your choice needs your own reason.
fabric_models: Model: fairly firm, little stretch, cut edge does not fray.
May support the cards and avoid a fraying edge. Test the actual sample.
Model: folds easily, little stretch across the weave, cut edge may fray.
May need edge finishing and support to keep its shape. Test the actual sample.
Model: stretches, may curl at a cut edge, shape can change when pulled.
May be harder to measure and hold steady. Test the actual sample.
fabric_note: These descriptions and the supplied photo are model information. Real fabrics vary. If you test an actual sample, record its real result. If no sample is available, write model information used; do not claim a test.
tests: With adult approval, hold a sample gently at two edges. Pull lightly across it, then release. Does it return to its shape?
Look at a cut edge. Does it shed threads, stay firm or curl? Do not pull threads out.
Bend the sample gently. Could it support three cards without flopping? Keep this as a prediction until the pouch is made.
techniques: Small passes through both fabric layers join the sides and bottom.
Needs an approved needle, thread and close adult supervision. Default route for this pouch.
A suitable adhesive may join the layers.
Adult must approve the actual label, fabric use and method. Wait for full cure before testing. No guessed cure time, heat or solvents.
A fastening can close an opening.
It does not replace joined sides and bottom. Our open-top pouch needs no fastening. Any change needs a revised approved design.
safety: Wait for adult approval before handling needles, scissors or adhesive. Use only the agreed tools and supervision.
Count needles out and back into a safe container. Never put pins or needles in your mouth or leave them in a product.
For a pause, put tools down in the agreed place. Keep fingers clear of a needle exit point. Tell the adult about a lost or damaged tool.
Use adhesive only after the adult checks the actual label and fabric. Follow the full cure instructions before testing. No heat, irons or solvent route is taught.
Today is choosing and planning. A model picture or empty-hand rehearsal does not prove textile testing or making.
fallback: With no fabric, tools, paper or printer, hear the purpose and model descriptions. Point, speak or sign a choice. Explain one property and one reason. Rehearse the plan with empty hands. An adult records exact confirmed words when a recording method is available. Mark transcription pending until it exists. Keep actual sample tests and textile making pending.
careers: Textile designers choose materials and joins to suit a user and a purpose. Testing a sample helps a maker explain a choice before cutting valuable material.

stages.name: Arrival
stages.title: A pouch with a job
pupil: Read or hear the purpose.
The pouch must hold three 60 mm by 80 mm cards.
Today we choose. Next week we measure and join.
stages.teacher: Show three actual cards if available, or describe their written size. Read the purpose and distinguish a useful item from decoration alone. Ask who will use it and what it must hold. Explain the top stays open. No personal possessions need to be shown. Use the last minute for a calm settling pause.
stages.check: Ask what must be joined and what stays open. Expect sides and bottom joined, top open. Re-read the brief if the opening is unclear.

stages.name: Starter
stages.title: What can a fabric do
pupil: Compare stretch, cut edge and firmness.
Use actual samples only with adult approval.
No samples means model information, not a test.
stages.teacher: Offer generic felt, woven cotton and stretch knit samples, or the labelled model photo and notes. Model gentle handling. Real samples may differ from the model descriptions. Read the three property checks. Choose one actual sample test if available; stop before any sharp tool is needed.
stages.check: Ask: Is a photo a test of your sample? No. Name actual sample evidence separately from model information.

stages.name: I do
stages.title: A choice with a reason
pupil: Watch a model choice linked to the purpose.
Compare stitching, bonding and a fastening.
Keep the top open.
stages.teacher: Model: I choose the felt model and hand running stitch because firm fabric may support the cards and stitch joins sides and bottom. Point to two rectangles 100 by 120 mm and the 10 mm side and bottom seam lines. This is a design plan, not a cutting demonstration. Compare adhesive approval and full cure against controlled needle use. A fastening closes an opening; it does not join our sides and bottom. Fade the example by leaving the final reason for the pupil to finish.
stages.check: Ask why a button alone is insufficient. Expect it does not join the sides and bottom. A quiz answer never authorises tool use.

stages.name: We do
stages.title: Compare a second choice
pupil: Could woven cotton suit this job?
Link a property to an effect.
Record a real test or name the model source.
stages.teacher: Compare felt and woven cotton together. A softer fabric may need support; a fraying edge may need finishing. Accept a different conclusion if it follows an actual sample result and an approved design. Use the frame property, effect, decision. An adult can read back a pupil explanation. No invented tests. Pupils may rehearse in any language or point to one property row.
stages.check: Ask for a property and a reason tied to the cards. A colour preference can be included, but it does not replace evidence about holding the cards.

stages.name: We do 2
stages.title: A join or a fastening
pupil: A button closes the top. Does it join both sides and bottom?
Choose yes, no, or only if it looks strong.
Explain the open-top design.
stages.teacher: Hinge answer is no. A fastening has a different job. If any pupil confuses the two, use two pieces or empty hands to point to sides, bottom and top. Parallel check: adhesive feels dry; may you test the join before the label cure is complete? No. Adult label approval and full cure are required. Recheck after reteaching.
stages.check: Move on when the pupil distinguishes joining from closing and explains one control for the chosen technique. If not, use Supported with the taught hand-stitch model and adult-led comparison.

stages.name: Independent
stages.title: My design decision
pupil: In your book, choose a fabric and joining method.
Give a property and a reason linked to the cards.
Sketch two 100 mm by 120 mm pieces and name the 10 mm seam lines.
Record actual sample testing or model information used.
stages.teacher: Use one route and the design decision prompts. The core decision may use model information honestly. Default felt and running stitch is available; the pupil still gives an own-word reason. A revised fabric or method needs adult review of dimensions, joining and safe access before Week 5. Use the last minute to check and organise the record.
stages.check: Check fabric, source of property evidence, join, purpose reason and dimensions. Scribe exact words and read back where needed. Missing tests remain pending; a valid reason based on model information can still show choosing.

stages.name: Review
stages.title: Check the choice against the job
pupil: Does the design hold the three cards?
Are the sides and bottom joined and the top open?
Keep one useful change or question.
stages.teacher: Offer a private adult check or a peer comment by consent. Review the plan rather than claiming the unmade item passed a load test. Confirm the actual design and any access changes for Week 5. The adult approves tools separately. Use the last minute for calm tidy and return any sample or tool.
stages.check: Pupil confirms their final choice and corrects any scribed words. Mark adult design review approved or pending. Record only actions that occurred.

stages.name: Exit
stages.title: My reason for the next maker
pupil: I choose ___ because ___.
I will join the sides and bottom using ___.
My evidence is an actual sample result or model information.
stages.teacher: Ask for a short pupil-owned choice and reason, privately if preferred. Keep the book location and actual support. Return and count any needles if they were demonstrated. Next week retrieves this exact design; an unfinished decision remains marked unfinished.
stages.check: The final evidence is a design decision with a purpose-linked reason and honest source label. It is not a claim of making or testing an entire pouch.

Supported: Use the felt model and hand running stitch, or choose after hearing two options.
Point to one helpful property. Say how it helps hold the cards.
Use the written dimensions: two pieces 100 mm by 120 mm, 10 mm seam lines.
Say your own reason. Name a real test or model information.
Standard: Compare two fabrics using stretch, edge and firmness.
Choose a fabric and join. Link one property to the pouch purpose.
Record the two piece sizes and three seam lines. Keep the top open.
Name your evidence source and one change or question.
Stretch: Complete the core design decision first.
Compare all three fabrics and two joining methods.
Explain a trade-off between firmness, stretch, edge finish and safe making.
Justify a rejected option and a useful later test. Do not claim a test you have not done.

vocabulary: The job the item needs to do.
A feature of a material, such as stretch or firmness.
When threads come loose at a cut edge.
Connect two parts so they stay together.
The line where two fabric parts are joined.
A part that closes an opening, such as a button and loop.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Read one property at a time. Compare two options before three. Model property, effect and decision, then fade to a sentence start. Keep written dimensions beside the sketch. Offer a repeated checklist.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Accept pointing, speech, signing and pupil-directed scribing. Give thinking time and a choice before an open question. Read the final choice back for correction.
adaptations.SEMH: Keep choices about an invented useful item. No personal hardship, body or spending disclosures. Offer private review and a calm pause. Put tools down before a pause and agree the safe return.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Offer no-touch comparison, a large view and adult handling of samples. Do not force texture contact. Plan the actual grip, tool and needle support before later making. A visual model does not prove a tactile test.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Match fabric words to the sample or labelled model. Use property, effect and decision as short spoken chunks. Preserve the pupil meaning in confirmed scribing.
